opus_only: A market-neutral cross-asset portfolio removes the dominant first principal component (the market), so it only harvests predictability in the remaining factors.
Footnote 1: forwards and futures are treated as equivalent in the theory section (ignores marking-to-market differences).
Breeden (1986) is cited for equilibrium links between interest rates and growth, used later to define rates value.
The value premium has rational and behavioural explanations, as momentum does.
The recent euro fall after surprise ECB easing illustrates overshooting; such moves create value opportunities in slow-adjusting assets such as euro-denominated real estate, which stayed sticky.
Each normalised crossover passes through R(z) = z*exp(-z^2/4)/0.89, which peaks near |z| = 1.4 and fades for extreme values; the final signal is the equal-weight (1/3) average over the three speeds.
Footnote 4: GDP growth enters with a three-month lag to approximate publication delay.
Example: equity value is long the three highest-yield indices and short the three lowest, held one business day.
Footnote 6: commodity carry relation F/S = exp((r + s - c)(T - t)), with s storage cost and c convenience yield.
Unlike the CS book, the time-series book can carry net directional exposure to an asset class when signals agree.
Directional equity carry and value both buy after falls and sell after rallies, hence negative equity betas; FX carry stays pro-cyclical.
TS equity value and equity carry correlate 51%, i.e. they are largely the same trade.
TS V+C+M 3-year rolling Sharpe falls to about 0.1 around 1999-2000 and peaks about 2.6 in 1997 and ~2.4 in 2003.
CS+TS style correlations also swing (carry-momentum up to ~0.75 around 1992; value-carry down to ~-0.55).
CS+TS 3-year rolling Sharpe ranges about 0.55 (around 1999-2000) to 2.6 (1997).
Rates universe: 10Y swaps for EUR, GBP, JPY, USD, NZD, AUD, CHF, CAD, NOK, SEK, HUF, PLN, ZAR, PHP (Bloomberg tickers like USSWAP10), starting 1988-2001.
sonnet_only: Practice differs: cash equity momentum is traded cross-sectionally, futures momentum directionally; the authors ask why and test both implementations.
Headline: the three styles are largely profitable and the combination of styles performs best.
The yield differential can pay for peso-problem jump risk that has not materialised in the sample, so realised carry returns may overstate safety.
Normal backwardation (Keynes): producers sell futures for insurance, creating structural excess futures supply so curves are backwardated and futures roll up to spot.
Empirically commodity curves are often not backwardated, so the Keynesian insurance story is incomplete.
Momentum explanations are split between risk-based (sensitivity to macro factors) and behavioural (underreaction/overreaction).
Alternative: prices overreact and feed on themselves via noise traders, deepening mispricing until a reversal.
Response function R(x)=x*exp(-x^2/4)/0.89 dampens extreme signals; u_k=R(z_k); final signal is equal-weighted (1/3) sum of u_k.
Combined TS and CS Sharpe ratios are similar (1.37 vs 1.40) though individual style performance differs a lot (CS strong in value, TS strong in momentum).

Reference list: Asness-Moskowitz-Pedersen (2013) value and momentum everywhere; Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen (2012) time series momentum; Koijen et al. (2013) Carry; Harvey-Liu-Zhu factor proliferation; Erb-Harvey (2006) commodities.
